overview: Qantas Airways is Australia's flag carrier and the parent of a dual-brand airline group spanning the full-service Qantas brand and the low-cost Jetstar brand, operating domestic, regional and international passenger services alongside a freight business and the Qantas Loyalty frequent flyer program. The Group operates 372 aircraft (FY2026) and carried almost 56 million passengers in FY2026, with the majority of capacity and earnings generated in the Australian domestic market and trans-Pacific/Asian international routes. Qantas is undergoing the largest fleet renewal program in its history, including ultra-long-haul Project Sunrise aircraft, while recycling capital out of loss-making offshore joint ventures (Jetstar Asia, Jetstar Japan) back into its core Australian and New Zealand businesses.

business_model.summary: Qantas earns the large majority of revenue from scheduled passenger airfares across four operating segments (Qantas Domestic, Qantas International/Freight, Jetstar Group, Qantas Loyalty), supplemented by freight and a high-margin, capital-light loyalty/financial-services business. Passenger revenue is largely transactional and cyclical, while Qantas Loyalty generates more recurring, annuity-like earnings from points-earning partnerships (banks, retail, insurance, home loans) and points redemption economics (the 'earn and burn flywheel').

revenue_streams.name: Qantas International (incl. Freight)
revenue_streams.trend: growing revenue, margin under pressure from fuel/FX

revenue_streams.name: Qantas Domestic
revenue_streams.trend: stable, margin compressed by fuel and corporate demand softness

revenue_streams.name: Qantas Loyalty
revenue_streams.trend: growing strongly, highest-margin segment (~22% EBIT margin)

business_model.customer_type: B2C leisure and premium travelers, B2B/government corporate accounts (Qantas Domestic ~79% corporate, ~53% SME share), B2B freight/e-commerce logistics customers, and loyalty program partners (banks, retailers, insurers)
business_model.geographic_mix: Predominantly Australia/New Zealand domestic and regional, with international long-haul to Asia, the Americas, Europe and the UK via Perth/Darwin and planned non-stop Sydney-London/New York routes (Project Sunrise); FY2026 Group Domestic ASKs 56,521M vs Group International ASKs 101,436M

main_competitors: International long-haul carriers (Singapore Airlines, Emirates, Cathay Pacific) on Asia/Europe routes
Other loyalty/rewards providers and financial institutions competing for Qantas Loyalty wallet share
competitive_position.market_position: Co-leader of an Australian domestic duopoly with Virgin Australia; ACCC data (Jan 2026) shows domestic market share roughly split evenly between Qantas (~33%), Jetstar (~33%) combined and Virgin Australia (~33%), with the duopoly controlling nearly 99% of domestic capacity. Internationally Qantas is a mid-sized long-haul carrier reliant on its home market and alliance/codeshare partnerships (e.g. with American Airlines, Japan Airlines, Emirates).

moat_factors.description: Only two major domestic groups control nearly all Australian capacity, supporting rational capacity discipline and pricing versus more fragmented markets

18.9 million members, 242 billion points earned in FY2026, deep bank/retail/insurance partnerships (>35% share of new points-earning credit cards) create switching costs and a high-margin annuity-like earnings stream
Qantas (premium) and Jetstar (low-cost) brands let the Group address the full fare spectrum and redeploy capacity between brands in response to demand shocks
Sydney Airport curfew and slot caps, and scarce international landing rights, raise barriers to new entrants on key routes
Largest Australian airline brand with extensive domestic network and lounge infrastructure, though repeated scandals have damaged brand trust

weaknesses: Reputational damage from the COVID-era illegal outsourcing/sacking of ~1,800 ground staff, the flight-credits scandal, and the July 2025 cyber breach has eroded public trust
High fixed-cost, labour- and fuel-intensive cost structure with limited near-term flexibility to offset input cost shocks
Heavily unionized workforce with a history of contentious industrial relations and enterprise bargaining disputes
Aging A380/A330 fleet carries rising maintenance costs ahead of retirement (A380 from CY2028, A330/737 by mid-2030s)
Virgin Australia's resurgence under new ownership/listing has pushed Qantas's once-dominant domestic share down to near-parity

growth_drivers: Project Sunrise: 12 A350-1000ULR ultra-long-haul aircraft (first deliveries from CY2027, five by Nov 2027) enabling non-stop Sydney-London and Sydney-New York services, targeted at ~$400 million of annual EBIT uplift at scale

Largest fleet renewal program in Group history (A220, A321XLR, A321LR, A320neo, 787-9/10) lowering unit costs and lifting NPS; new-technology aircraft ~30% of narrowbody ASKs in FY2026, with ~70% of Group ASKs expected to be next-generation by FY2030/31 and premium cabin mix rising from 19% to 28% of ASKs

Qantas Loyalty monetization: expansion of Qantas Business Rewards (706,000+ members, +11% YoY), Financial Services (credit cards, home loans, insurance), and new retail partnerships (David Jones, Uber, Ticketek) driving double-digit EBIT growth

Capital recycling out of lower-returning offshore ventures (Jetstar Asia closure, Jetstar Japan divestment to JAL/DBJ) to redeploy capital into higher-returning core Qantas/Jetstar Australian and New Zealand operations

Network expansion into new domestic and international leisure routes (e.g. Western Sydney Airport launch, new Jetstar international routes to Cebu, Colombo, Queenstown, Rarotonga, Denpasar) and resilient premium international demand

business.description: Virgin Australia has reached near-parity domestic market share, pressuring yields and capacity discipline in the historically rational duopoly
Illegal ground-staff outsourcing, the COVID flight-credits class action, and the 2025 cyber breach have damaged customer trust and invited regulatory and legal action
Large unionized workforce and Fair Work Act changes create risk of enterprise bargaining disputes and industrial action
A worker fatality at the Sydney freight terminal in September 2025 triggered a SafeWork NSW investigation and a zeroed safety bonus scorecard
AI-driven search and booking tools could erode direct customer engagement and loyalty program relevance over time

financial.description: The Middle East conflict alone drove a ~$610 million gross fuel cost increase ($420 million net of hedging) in FY2026, and 1H FY2027 fuel bill is now guided at ~$3.75 billion
Fuel, aircraft leases and overseas operations (e.g. Jetstar Japan) are exposed to AUD volatility; FX losses on Jetstar Japan lease liabilities reduced equity-accounted earnings in FY2026

financial.risk: Negative free cash flow / high capex
financial.description: FY2026 Net Free Cash Flow was negative $75 million as net capex rose to $3,968 million; FY2027 net capex is guided at $4.3-4.6 billion, pressuring balance sheet flexibility if conditions worsen
Net Debt increased to $6.2 billion (mid-point of the $5.5-6.9 billion target range) in FY2026, up from $5.0 billion in FY2025

regulatory.description: Political and regulatory shifts could materially affect bargaining flexibility and operating costs

ACCC scrutiny of the domestic duopoly and consumer protection enforcement following the flight-credits case ($105 million settlement, pending Federal Court approval) and ground-handling case ($90 million penalty)
Targets include 25% Scope 1+2 emissions reduction from 2019 levels by 2030, 10% SAF usage by 2030, and net zero by 2050; policy shifts on SAF mandates or carbon pricing could raise costs
Despite the 2025 cyber breach, the OAIC closed its preliminary inquiry without finding a privacy law breach or taking further action, reducing (but not eliminating) regulatory tail risk

macro.description: The Middle East conflict disrupted global routings and spiked fuel prices through FY2026, directly costing the Group ~$420 million net
Cost-of-living pressure and economic uncertainty reduced large-corporate and government travel demand in Q4 FY2026; travel demand is discretionary and sensitive to recession risk
Capital-intensive fleet financing (debt and aircraft leases) makes financing costs sensitive to interest rate moves, though the Baa2 investment-grade rating helps contain funding costs

execution.description: First-of-type ultra-long-haul A350-1000ULR program carries delivery, certification and ramp-up risk ahead of the ~$400 million EBIT uplift target
Closure of Jetstar Asia (completed July 2025) and the pending Jetstar Japan divestment to JAL/DBJ (targeted completion by June 2027) require successful capital recycling and fleet/staff redeployment
CEO Vanessa Hudson and a substantially renewed Board (six of nine directors joined since 2023) continue to rebuild trust and operational performance after the pandemic-era scandals

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Australian domestic aviation remains a stable, rational duopoly with near-full capacity utilization; international long-haul demand is resilient in premium cabins, though global aviation remains exposed to geopolitical shocks (Middle East conflict) that can spike fuel costs and disrupt routings industry-wide
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate-to-high - passenger and freight revenue are sensitive to consumer discretionary spending, corporate travel budgets and broader economic conditions, partially offset by the more defensive, recurring Qantas Loyalty segment
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate - large debt and aircraft lease balances funding an extensive fleet renewal program make financing costs sensitive to rate moves, mitigated by an investment-grade (Moody's Baa2) credit rating
key_input_costs: Labour costs under enterprise bargaining agreements
Airport and aviation charges (rising faster than CPI)

recent_developments.event: Major cyber incident exposed personal data of approximately 5.7-6 million customers; stolen data was later leaked online (Oct 2025); executive bonuses cut 15% in response
Federal Court imposed a record $90 million penalty (on top of ~$120 million in compensation agreed Dec 2024) for the Group's illegal outsourcing and sacking of ~1,700-1,800 ground staff during COVID
A worker died at the Sydney freight terminal; the Board zeroed the workplace safety component of FY2026 short-term bonuses pending a SafeWork NSW investigation
Non-binding MOU signed with Japan Airlines on restructuring Jetstar Japan's ownership; Board announced (but later shelved) a $150 million on-market share buy-back
Qantas agreed to pay A$105 million, without admission of liability, to settle the COVID-era flight credits class action, subject to Federal Court approval

FY2026 results: Underlying PBT of $2,064 million (down 13.8% YoY) and Statutory Profit After Tax of $1,289 million (down 19.7%), reflecting a ~$420 million net impact from Middle East conflict-driven fuel costs; decided not to proceed with the $150 million buy-back; approved a $300 million fully franked final dividend (19.8 cents/share)

Signed a binding agreement with Japan Airlines to divest the Group's 33.32% Jetstar Japan stake via a ~JPY8.2 billion share buy-back, with an estimated ~A$115 million gain and completion targeted by June 2027; Jetstar Japan will rebrand away from 'Jetstar'

AGM trading update (6 Nov) reaffirmed FY2026-results guidance: 1H FY2027 Total Unit Revenue (TRASK) growth of 8-10%, Group Domestic capacity down ~3% in 1H FY2027, Qantas Loyalty EBIT growth of 5-7% in FY2027, and FY2027 net capex trending to the lower end of $4.3-4.6 billion, against a raised 1H FY2027 fuel bill estimate of ~$3.75 billion

Broker reaction mixed: CLSA cut its target to A$10.74 (from A$12.90) and Jarden to A$10.20, while UBS raised to A$11.60 and Morgan Stanley maintained a A$12.80 target; shares traded around A$10 in mid-November 2026, below most analyst targets

guidance.as_of: FY2026 Results (27 Aug 2026) and AGM Trading Update (6 Nov 2026)

items.notes: Reaffirmed at the November 2026 AGM trading update; 2H FY2027 TRASK guidance due with 1H FY2027 results in February 2027
Reflects capacity discipline in response to elevated fuel costs and softer large-corporate/government demand
Continuation of double-digit-adjacent growth trend (12% in FY2026) at a more moderate pace

items.target: $4.3-4.6 billion, trending to the lower end
items.notes: Funds continued fleet renewal including Project Sunrise aircraft deliveries
Reflects elevated fuel prices following the Middle East conflict; most of the half-year's fuel requirement already hedged
Expected to rise over time as Invested Capital grows with continued fleet investment
FY2026 ROIC was 32.2%, down from 50.8% in FY2025; management expects ROIC to moderate toward more sustainable levels as Invested Capital rebuilds from COVID-depressed levels

items.target: approximately $400 million annual EBIT uplift at scale
items.notes: First of 12 A350-1000ULR aircraft entering service from calendar year 2027; five expected by November 2027

guidance.management_commentary: Chair John Mullen and CEO Vanessa Hudson both emphasized the resilience of the Group's integrated portfolio (dual-brand airlines plus Qantas Loyalty) in absorbing the ~$420 million Middle East conflict impact while continuing to invest in fleet renewal and customer experience. At the November 2026 AGM update, management said trading remained in line with the outlook provided at the August FY2026 results, despite the higher 1H FY2027 fuel bill, and reiterated that Qantas is 'well placed to shape the next era of aviation' given its fleet renewal program, loyalty program strength and investment-grade balance sheet.

bull_case: Domestic duopoly structure with Virgin Australia supports rational capacity and pricing discipline, underpinning structurally higher margins than most global airline markets
Qantas Loyalty is a high-margin (~22% EBIT margin), capital-light, recurring-revenue business growing EBIT at a double-digit pace, providing an earnings stabilizer against airline cyclicality
The largest fleet renewal program in Group history is lowering unit costs and lifting customer satisfaction, with next-generation aircraft expected to reach ~70% of Group ASKs by FY2030/31
Project Sunrise gives Qantas a first-mover position in non-stop ultra-long-haul premium travel (Sydney-London/New York), targeted at ~$400 million of incremental annual EBIT at scale
Disciplined Financial Framework (Net Debt/EBITDA targets, ROIC > WACC, investment-grade Baa2 rating) and capital recycling out of loss-making offshore ventures support continued shareholder returns

Current analyst price targets (consensus roughly A$10.9-11.5, up to A$12.80 from Morgan Stanley) sit above the mid-November 2026 trading price of roughly A$10, implying potential upside if fuel costs normalize
bear_case: Heavy, largely uncontrollable fuel price and FX exposure: the Middle East conflict alone cost ~$420 million net in FY2026 and pushed the 1H FY2027 fuel bill to ~$3.75 billion

Repeated reputational and legal setbacks - the $90 million ground-handling penalty, the $105 million flight-credits settlement, and the 2025 cyber breach affecting ~5.7-6 million customers - continue to weigh on brand trust and invite further scrutiny
Virgin Australia's resurgence has pushed Qantas's once-dominant domestic market share down to near-parity (~33% each per ACCC data), intensifying competitive and pricing pressure

Large, multi-year fleet capex program ($4.3-4.6 billion guided for FY2027) drove FY2026 Net Free Cash Flow negative (-$75 million) and could strain the balance sheet if demand or fuel conditions worsen

Margin compression is already visible - Group Operating Margin fell from 11.1% to 9.2% and Qantas International margin nearly halved to ~4% in FY2026 - highlighting the Group's operating leverage to external shocks
Unionized, labour-intensive cost base and history of contentious industrial relations create ongoing risk of enterprise bargaining disputes or industrial action
